sn55.21:1.4: _Byūha_ (“cul-de-sac”) is defined in the Vinaya: “one departs the same way one enters” ([pli-tv-bi-vb-pc14:2.1.8]()).
sn55.21:1.13: This relates to the commonly-held idea in modern Theravada that rebirth is determined by one’s “last mind-moment” or “final thought”. This idea is incorrect on a number of grounds. First, there’s no such thing as “mind moments” in early Buddhism. Second, rebirth is determined not by “thought” (_citta_) but by “deed” (_kamma_). So it would only apply in the case of someone who was actually committing good or bad kamma at the time of death, which most people are not, like Mahānāma here; he is simply returning home. Finally, what normally prevails at the time of death is habitual _kamma_ (like keeping precepts every day) or very strong _kamma_ (such as attaining _jhāna_). In the Suttas, deathbed _kamma_ prevails only in rare cases when someone is creating very good ([mn97:38.7]()) or very bad ([sn42.3:2.7]()) _kamma_ at the time of death; see too the case of Sarakāni in [sn55.24:9.11]() and [sn55.25:11.10]().
sn55.21:3.2: There is a parallel for this simile at [sn42.6:7.1]().
sn55.21:3.5: Here _citta_ (“mind”) continues from one life to the next, in the role that _viññāṇa_ plays elsewhere (eg. [dn28:7.13]()).
